E_aggregated.action_count_comment: No official tool-reference page, names, schemas, or stated total was found in Crypto.com’s official docs or public repository. Agentman’s third-party page reports nine tools and supplies the lowercase names used in actions.json; parameters are not published there. Anthropic’s Claude connector directory lists nine names, but capitalizes get_candlestick, get_tickers, get_ticker, and get_book differently; it is a third-party listing. MCP.so reports nine tools; Tooljunction is another catalogue but did not provide a separate verified count in the reviewed text. No catalogue-only tools were added beyond the nine-tool inventory.

E_aggregated.token_method: The public repository is a separate agent skill/CLI project, not the hosted MCP implementation; official tool definitions and initialize instructions were not published verbatim. The third-party snapshot does not expose complete serialized schemas.
E_aggregated.human_can_agent_cannot: Official docs state the MCP does not execute trades or transactions, provide financial advice, predict future prices, or access personal accounts or wallets. Those operations or information are outside this market-data server. Source: https://mcp.crypto.com/docs/features

F_documentation.implementation_hints_not_enforced: The official FAQ suggests making requests explicit with words such as “CURRENT”, “now”, “today”, or “latest” when the assistant does not recognize the need for current data. These are client/user recommendations; no server enforcement is documented. Source: https://mcp.crypto.com/docs/faq
F_documentation.governance_promises: Official FAQ claims the server “Doesn’t collect or store your personal information”, “Doesn’t access your conversations”, and “nothing is stored or tracked.” The official features page says it only provides public market data and cannot access personal accounts or wallets. Source: https://mcp.crypto.com/docs/faq
F_documentation.promises_to_user: Official docs describe the service as free, requiring no account or API key, with real-time market data refreshed every few seconds. They say it can be removed or disabled through the client. Sources: https://mcp.crypto.com/docs/getting-started, https://mcp.crypto.com/docs/features, https://mcp.crypto.com/docs/faq
F_documentation.comparison_with_server_logic: The public-data-only scope and no-trading claims are consistent with the reported read-only tool annotations. No hosted implementation is public, so storage, tracking, retention, and rate-limit implementation cannot be independently verified from code. The privacy dashboard provides jurisdiction-specific notices but the reviewed page does not specifically describe this MCP service.

contradictions: Anthropic’s third-party directory lists nine tools but capitalizes four names (`Get_candlestick`, `Get_tickers`, `Get_ticker`, `Get_book`); Agentman’s 2026-08-17 reported tools/list snapshot uses lowercase names. MCP names are case-sensitive, according to Agentman.

Agentman reports the server initialize instructions mention `get_widget`, `get_market_orderbook`, `get_market_trades`, and `get_market_candles`, while its tools/list snapshot contains nine different tool names and no such names. Crypto.com’s docs do not publish the initialize instructions or a tool list to resolve this discrepancy.

A supplied endpoint POST returned HTTP 406 because the client did not accept both application/json and text/event-stream; the input separately records a successful HTTP 200 initialize test. The supplied metadata requests for protected-resource and authorization-server well-known URLs returned HTTP 404. These observations concern different request conditions and do not establish OAuth support.
observations_for_research: This endpoint is documented as public market-data access without authentication, while the same vendor’s public Exchange agent-skill repository describes a distinct CLI workflow for account, order, and wallet operations; those separate capabilities are not in this endpoint’s action inventory.
The docs encourage natural-language use but do not publish the machine-readable tool descriptions or schemas, leaving the reported tool inventory dependent on third-party snapshots.
The reported server instructions may contain stale tool identifiers that could guide an agent toward unavailable calls; this is based on a third-party comparison, not an official reproduction.
